stops.name: Tyre, a daughter of the house of Belus
stops.campa: Tyre stands on her rock in the sea, mistress of the purple dye-vats and the cedar road to Egypt, when a daughter is born to the king the Tyrians call Belus, or Mattan. The priests name her Elissa; later ages, remembering how far she wandered, will call her Dido, 'the wanderer.' She grows up under the bell of Melqart's temple and the reek of the murex pits, clever, pious, and already marked, the annals say, as fit to rule better than any woman, or most men, of her house.

stops.name: Tyre, the death of Belus, the throne given to Pygmalion
stops.campa: The old king dies and leaves the throne of Tyre to his son and daughter jointly, but the people will not be governed by a woman and set the boy Pygmalion, still a child, alone on the seat. Elissa does not contest it. She takes the immense dowry of her house instead and gives her hand to Acerbas, her own uncle, priest of Melqart-Hercules, a man of such fortune that he trusts no wall to hold it and buries the greater part of his gold in the earth, telling no one but her.

stops.name: Tyre, the altar, and the murder of Acerbas
stops.campa: Pygmalion, grown to manhood and hungry for gold beyond what a kingdom yields, learns of his brother-in-law's buried hoard and is seized, the histories say, by a greed that puts out every family feeling. He strikes Acerbas down in secret, before the very altars of the god he serves, and thinks the killing hidden, for Elissa is his sister, and he trusts her grief to be private and her silence assured. He has not reckoned with what a wronged wife can do with a fleet, a treasury, and half the senate of Tyre behind her.

stops.name: Tyre, the ghost of Sychaeus reveals the gold and the crime
stops.campa: Where the histories give her cunning, the poets give her a vision: the unburied ghost of her husband, Sychaeus in the Roman telling, comes to her in sleep, lifts the veil from his own wounds, and lays bare the altar's crime and her brother's hand in it. He shows her ancient treasure hidden in the earth, a weight of gold and silver known to no one else alive, and tells her to take it and flee the country. She wakes knowing what must be done, and grieves alone, trusting no face at court, not even her own reflection.
stops.quote: Auxiliumque viae veteres tellure recludit / thesauros, ignotum argenti pondus et auri.
stops.quote_source: Virgil, Aeneid 1.358-359 (the ghost unearths the ancient hoard, 'an unknown weight of silver and gold')

stops.name: Tyre, the sacks of sand and the gathering of the conspirators
stops.campa: Elissa feigns reconciliation, tells her brother she wishes to move into his own house so the sight of her husband's rooms will no longer grieve her, and asks for men to help the removal. By night she loads bags of common sand aboard the waiting ships, calling them Acerbas's gold, and has them cast into the sea as an offering to appease his shade, so that the attendants, thinking themselves already accomplices in a fortune thrown to the deep, dare not turn back to Pygmalion. She wins over the frightened men and a company of the city's senators to sail with her before dawn.
stops.quote: That he would favourably receive his wealth which he had left behind him, and accept that as an offering to his shade.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.4 (trans. J. S. Watson; her entreaty to Acerbas as the sand goes into the sea)

stops.name: Tyre harbor, the fleet slips away, and the augurs stay Pygmalion's hand
stops.campa: At first light the ships stand out from Tyre's harbor, Elissa at the head of a company of nobles, priests, and common folk who will not stay under a brother's hand stained with murder. Pygmalion, told of the flight and the vanished treasury, orders pursuit, until his augurs, reading the sky, warn him that he will not go unpunished if he breaks off the founding of a city fated to become the most prosperous in the world. He lets his sister go, more from fear of the gods than love of her, and Tyre's exiles turn their prows toward the setting sun.
stops.quote: He would not escape with impunity, if he interrupted the founding of a city that was to become the most prosperous in the whole world.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.4 (trans. J. S. Watson, of Pygmalion's augurs)

stops.name: Cyprus, the priest of Jupiter joins his fortune to hers
stops.campa: The fleet's first landfall is Cyprus, where the priest of Jupiter, of Baal in the Tyrian tongue, comes to the shore with his wife and children and offers himself as Elissa's companion, prompted, the histories say, by the gods themselves, on the condition that the priesthood remain forever with his line in whatever city she builds. She takes him gladly: a colony needs an altar as much as a wall, and a priest's blessing will steady the frightened company for the crossing still ahead of them into open, unknown water.
stops.quote: At the instigation of the gods, as her companion and the sharer of her fortunes.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.5 (trans. J. S. Watson)

stops.name: Cyprus, the eighty women taken for wives
stops.campa: Custom on this shore sets young women apart for a season by the sea before their marriages, to earn a dowry and honor the goddess with their bodies before they belong to one man alone. Elissa, needing wives for a company of exiles who have left their own women in Tyre, orders some eighty of them seized and brought aboard, that her men might have households and her city, from its first hour, a people to grow rather than a garrison to dwindle. Weeping and protest give way, by the time the ships clear the roads, to the business of survival.
stops.quote: That her men might have wives, and her city a population.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.5 (trans. J. S. Watson)

stops.name: The open sea, the long road west along Sicily's shore
stops.campa: From Cyprus the ships run the length of the sea her people already know as traders: past Rhodes and Crete, along the Sicilian coast where later ages will remember a Tyrian queen once touched land, and out at last across the open water toward Libya, where Utica, an older colony of Tyre, already stands. Elissa keeps her council small: the priest of Baal, the senators who fled with her, the memory of Sychaeus never far from her prayers. She does not yet know what shore will let her land, only that Pygmalion's reach ends at the horizon behind her.

stops.name: The Libyan coast, Utica's welcome, kin to kin
stops.campa: The exiles make land at last on the Gulf of Tunis, and the people of Utica, themselves children of Tyre settled here a generation before, come down to the shore not as strangers but as family, sending gifts and urging the newcomers to build where they have chosen. The native Libyans of the country, glad of the trade a Tyrian city will bring, likewise welcome them and are willing to sell land. Elissa asks only for ground enough to shelter her weary company until she can, as she tells them, 'conveniently resume her progress', a modest word for what she intends.
stops.quote: As much as could be covered with an ox-hide, where she might refresh her companions, wearied with their long voyage.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.5 (trans. J. S. Watson)

stops.name: Byrsa Hill, the ox-hide cut into a thousand strips
stops.campa: The Libyan chiefs grant, laughing, as much ground as a single ox-hide can cover, a jest at a beggar-queen's expense. Elissa has the hide cut into strips as thin as thread and laid end to end around the whole shoulder of a hill above the bay, so that what was promised as a handkerchief of earth becomes a citadel. The Libyans, outwitted but bound by their own word, let the circuit stand. The hill takes the name Byrsa, 'the hide,' and every stone of the citadel that will one day face Rome rises first from this one measured lie.
stops.quote: She directed the hide to be cut into the thinnest possible strips, and thus acquired a greater portion of ground than she had apparently demanded.
stops.quote_source: Justin, Epitome of Pompeius Trogus 18.5 (trans. J. S. Watson)

stops.name: Byrsa, the ox-head and the horse-head, the site chosen
stops.campa: Digging the first foundations, the settlers turn up the head of an ox: a sign, the diviners say, of a rich but toiling and subject people, fit only to labor. Elissa will not build her city on that omen and orders the works moved. At the new ground the diggers find instead a horse's head, token of a nation strong in war and destined to rule; on this she founds Carthage in earnest, and the double meaning of the site, plenty bought at the price of arms, will hold true for six hundred years, down to the last siege.
